newsitem.title: USA: Ban sought on U.S. funds for assisted suicide.
newsitem.headline: Ban sought on U.S. funds for assisted suicide.

text.p: As the Supreme Court heard arguments on proposals to recognize a constitutional right to physician-assisted suicide, two U.S. senators said Wednesday they would seek a ban on using federal health programs to pay for such deaths.

A bill sponsored by Sen. Byron Dorgan, a North Dakota Democrat, and Sen. John Ashcroft, a Missouri Republican, does not address the legality or constitutionality of assisted suicide. The senators said that should be left to the courts and the states.
But it would prevent federal tax dollars from going to assisted suicide, primarily through Medicaid and Medicare. "This is a very targeted and limited effort on our part," Ashcroft said.

The two senators introduced a similar bill late in the last session of Congress, and plan to introduce it as soon as possible in the new Congress. Dorgan said the bill applied to assisted-suicide, and not to decisions to withhold medical treatment, life support, or nutrients from a dying person.
"We choose not to allow federal funds to be used to pay for physician-assisted suicide," Dorgan said. "It's as simple as that."

The Supreme Court Wednesday heard oral arguments on cases from New York and Washington state. A third assisted suicide law in Oregon is in lower courts, but state officials have said that if it goes into effect they would try to use Medicaid funds to pay for doctor-assisted suicide.
Advocates of assisted suicide said mentally competent, terminally ill patients should be allowed to ask their doctor for help in ending their lives to relieve needless pain and suffering.
But critics, including most major medical groups, said it was wrong to punish doctors who end the lives of their patients and said they feared it could lead to abuses.
